questions.solution: B is on Thursday, so the C–E pair is Mon–Tue, Tue–Wed or Fri–Sat, and D can't be on Wed or Fri. questions.question: With 20 coins, how many coins must Asha remove on her first turn to be sure of winning?
questions.solution: Work backwards: a pile is 'losing' for the player to move if every move leads to a winning pile. 0 is losing. 1, 2 and 4 can reach 0, so they're winning. 3 → 2 or 1 only, so it's losing. In general, the losing piles are exactly the multiples of 3, because 1, 2 and 4 are never multiples of 3. 20 − 2 = 18 is a multiple of 3. Taking 1 (19) or 4 (16) leaves a winning pile for Bilal.

questions.question: For how many starting pile sizes from 1 to 30 (inclusive) can Bilal force a win?
questions.solution: Work backwards: a pile is 'losing' for the player to move if every move leads to a winning pile. 0 is losing. 1, 2 and 4 can reach 0, so they're winning. 3 → 2 or 1 only, so it's losing. In general, the losing piles are exactly the multiples of 3, because 1, 2 and 4 are never multiples of 3. Bilal wins exactly when the start is a multiple of 3: 3, 6, …, 30, which is 10 sizes.

questions.question: Under the standard rule, what is the smallest starting pile larger than 20 with which Bilal can force a win?
questions.solution: Work backwards: a pile is 'losing' for the player to move if every move leads to a winning pile. 0 is losing. 1, 2 and 4 can reach 0, so they're winning. 3 → 2 or 1 only, so it's losing. In general, the losing piles are exactly the multiples of 3, because 1, 2 and 4 are never multiples of 3. The next multiple of 3 after 20 is 21.

questions.question: Suppose players may remove 1, 2, 3 or 4 coins (last coin still wins). With 23 coins, how many should Asha remove first to be sure of winning?
questions.solution: With moves 1–4, the losing piles are multiples of 5 (any move from 5k can be answered to return to 5(k − 1)). Asha should leave 20, so she takes 3.

questions.question: Now suppose the rule is reversed: the player who takes the last coin LOSES (moves are still 1, 2 or 4). With 10 coins, how many should Asha remove first to be sure of winning?
questions.solution: Now a pile of 1 is losing for the player to move, because they must take the last coin. Working upward: 2, 3 → can leave 1, so winning. 4 → leaves 3, 2 or 0, and 0 means you just took the last coin and lost, so 4 is losing. The losing piles are 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, … (one more than a multiple of 3). 10 is losing: from 10, Asha can leave 9, 8 or 6, and each lets Bilal move back to 7. So she cannot force a win.

questions.question: What number did S write in round 2?
questions.solution: Count scoring turns. R's 5 must come from two different numbers (1 + 4 or 2 + 3), so R scores in exactly two rounds; P, Q and S each score at least once. That is at least 5 scoring turns. A round with a repeated number has at most 2 scorers, and round 2 has exactly 1, so there are at most 2 + 1 + 2 = 5. Hence exactly 5: P scores once (4, in round 3), Q once (1), S once (2), R twice, and rounds 1 and 3 have two scorers each. Q wrote 4 in round 1 but scored only 1 overall, so Q did not score in round 1; P scored only in round 3. So the round-1 scorers are R and S, and Q's 4 was matched by P: round 1 is P 4, Q 4, S 2, R a with a = 1 or 3. If R scored again in round 3 (and Q in round 2), the totals of the numbers come out to 32 + 2b for a whole number b, never 33 — impossible. So Q scored 1 in round 3 and R scored alone in round 2 with 5 − a. If a = 3, R's numbers 3, 2 and his round-3 number (which must pair with S, avoiding 4 and 1) clash; so a = 1 and R wrote 4 in round 2. Round 2: P, Q, S wrote the same d; round 3: P 4, Q 1, R and S both c (c = 2 or 3). Sum: 11 + (3d + 4) + (5 + 2c) = 33 gives 3d + 2c = 13, so c = 2 and d = 3. Final: round 1 — P 4, Q 4, R 1, S 2; round 2 — P 3, Q 3, R 4, S 3; round 3 — P 4, Q 1, R 2, S 2. A computer check of all 4¹² possibilities confirms it is the only one.

questions.question: How many coins did A hold at the start?
questions.solution: The total, 160 coins, never changes. Work backwards from the end: in the round a player loses, every other player's holding is halved (undoing the doubling) and the loser gets back what he paid. Of the six orders with B first, only (B, D, A, C) and (B, A, D, C) leave C with the fewest coins at the start, and 'D before A' picks the first. Undoing the rounds for B, D, A, C gives starting holdings A 21, B 82, C 13, D 44. Forward check: after round 1 (B loses) 42, 4, 26, 88; after round 2 (D loses) 84, 8, 52, 16; after round 3 (A loses) 8, 16, 104, 32; after round 4 (C loses) 16, 32, 48, 64 ✓.

questions.question: How many bananas did X get?
questions.solution: Z's six fruits are apples plus equal numbers of oranges and bananas, so Z's apples = 6 − 2 × (Z's bananas), an even number. If Z had 2 or more apples, X would need at least 3 and Y at least 4, which is 9 or more apples, but there are only 7. So Z has 0 apples, 3 bananas and 3 oranges. X has no oranges, so the remaining 5 − 3 = 2 oranges are Y's. Y's other 4 fruits are apples and bananas, and X's 6 fruits are apples and bananas. X and Y share all 7 apples with Y having more: the splits (3, 4), (2, 5) and (1, 6) are possible in principle, but Y can hold at most 4 apples, so X has 3 apples and Y has 4. Then X has 6 − 3 = 3 bananas and Y has 0 bananas. Result: X 3 apples, 3 bananas, 0 oranges; Y 4 apples, 0 bananas, 2 oranges; Z 0 apples, 3 bananas, 3 oranges. A computer check of every possible split confirms this is the only one. X got 3 bananas.

b2-doubling.title: The doubling game (Hard)
b2-doubling.html:
The doubling game

Four players, A, B, C and D, play four rounds of a game with coins. Each round has exactly one loser, and every player loses exactly one round. The loser of a round pays each of the other three players as many coins as that player holds at that moment, so each of the other three doubles their holding. The loser always has enough coins to pay. No other coins change hands.

  • After the four rounds, A, B, C and D hold 16, 32, 48 and 64 coins respectively.
  • At the start, B held more coins than the other three put together.
  • At the start, C held fewer coins than each of the others.
  • D lost a round before A did.

b2-floors.title: Floors, pets and jobs (Medium)
b2-floors.html:
Floors, pets and jobs

Arjun, Bina, Chetan, Divya and Esha live on floors 1 to 5 of a building (floor 1 is the lowest), one person per floor. Each has a different pet — cat, dog, parrot, fish, rabbit — and a different job — doctor, lawyer, teacher, engineer, pilot.

  • The pilot lives above the dog owner, and the dog owner lives on the floor immediately above the teacher.
  • Arjun lives on the floor immediately below the rabbit owner.
  • The doctor lives on an odd-numbered floor and owns neither the cat nor the dog.
  • Bina lives on an even-numbered floor and is neither the teacher nor the pilot.
  • The fish owner lives exactly three floors below the dog owner.
  • The lawyer owns the cat.
  • Esha lives above Divya but below Bina.

b2-fruit.title: Sharing fruit (Easy)
b2-fruit.html:
Sharing fruit

Seven apples, six bananas and five oranges (18 fruits in all) are shared among three friends, X, Y and Z, so that each friend gets exactly six fruits. It is also known that:

  • X got no oranges.
  • Y got more apples than X, and X got more apples than Z.
  • Z got as many oranges as bananas.

b2-knights.title: Knights and knaves (Hard)
b2-knights.html:
Knights and knaves

On an island every inhabitant is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a knave, who always lies. Six inhabitants, A, B, C, D, E and F, make one statement each:

  • A: “B is a knave.”
  • B: “Exactly three of us six are knights.”
  • C: “D is a knave, or A is a knight.”
  • D: “E and F are of the same type.”
  • E: “A and D are of the same type.”
  • F: “C is a knave, or E is a knave.”

(“X or Y” is true when at least one of X, Y is true.)

b2-unique.title: The unique-number game (Hard)
b2-unique.html:
The unique-number game

Four players, P, Q, R and S, play three rounds of a game. In each round every player secretly writes a whole number from 1 to 4; different players may write the same number. When the numbers are revealed, a player scores the number he wrote if nobody else wrote that number in that round; otherwise he scores 0 for the round.

  • In every round, at least two players wrote the same number.
  • Q wrote 4 in round 1.
  • In round 2, exactly three players wrote the same number.
  • P scored in round 3.
  • R wrote a different number in each round.
  • At the end of the three rounds, the total scores were P 4, Q 1, R 5 and S 2.
  • The twelve numbers written add up to 33.

cd-choc.title: Sharing chocolates

Sharing chocolates

24 chocolates were shared among five friends P, Q, R, S and T. Each got at least one, and no two got the same number.

cd-coins.title: Coin game
cd-coins.html:
Coin game

Asha and Bilal play a game with a pile of coins. They take turns, Asha first. On each turn a player must remove 1, 2 or 4 coins (never more than the pile holds). Under the standard rule, the player who takes the last coin wins. Both players always play perfectly.

cd-houses.title: Four houses
